procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 29.04.2016 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in W.P. (Crl.) No.1003 of2016, directing the appellant to produce the daughter and comply with the orders passed by the U.K. Court or hand over the minor to the respondent-father within three weeks therefrom.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent (father) filed a writ petition before the High Court of Delhi against the appellant (wife) seeking a writ of habeas corpus for production of the minor before the Court. The High Court directed the appellant to produce the daughter and comply with the orders passed by the U.K. Court or hand over the minor to the respondent-father within three weeks therefrom.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (wife) appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court is hearing Criminal Appeal No. 968 of 2017.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the immediate restoration of the custody of the child to the respondent-mother without adequately examining the facts and circumstances bearing on the child's interest and welfare.

facts: The child was in the custody of the appellant-father.
The High Court had directed the immediate restoration of the child's custody to the respondent-mother.
The Supreme Court found no persuasive or convincing material on record to prove that an immediate restoration of custody to the mother was obligatorily required for the child's interest and welfare.
The Court noted that the appellant, being the biological father, could not be said to have illegal or unlawful custody of the child.
law: The sole and predominant criterion in custody matters is the interest and welfare of the minor child.

When a child is brought to India from another country, the Indian court must conduct its own inquiry (either summary or elaborate) into the child's welfare. The welfare of the child is the paramount consideration.

A pre-existing order from a foreign court is only one of the factors to be considered and should not be the sole basis for a decision. Principles like comity of courts are secondary to the child's welfare.

A writ of habeas corpus is not the appropriate remedy to enforce a foreign custody order when the child is in the lawful custody of a biological parent, unless a transfer is proven to be in the child's best interest.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court failed to apply the correct legal standard.
The High Court did not adequately examine the facts, circumstances, and other materials on record to determine what was in the child's best interest.
Instead of prioritizing the child's welfare, the High Court was wrongly impelled by the principle of comity of courts and doctrines of "intimate contact" and "closest concern".
The Supreme Court concluded that dislodging the child from the father's custody, as directed by the High Court, would be harmful to the child.
Since the father's custody was not illegal, the High Court's use of a habeas corpus writ to order the transfer was inappropriate without a thorough welfare analysis.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, finding it was not justified. The High Court erred by ordering the immediate restoration of the child's custody to the mother without conducting an adequate and independent examination of the facts and circumstances to determine if such a move was in the child's best interest, which is the paramount consideration in all custody matters.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the immediate restoration of the custody of the child to the respondent-mother without adequately examining the facts and circumstances bearing on the child's interest and welfare.
appellant_arguments: The petition for a writ of habeas corpus was misconceived as there was no imminent danger to the child's life or well-being.
An effective and efficacious remedy was already available and pending adjudication under the Guardian and Wards Act, 1890, so the writ petition should have been declined.
A summary adjudication is unmerited for a child custody issue, which requires a proper trial to be decided.
respondent_arguments: The child is an American citizen by birth, with Virginia as his home state.
The appellant had illegally detained the child in defiance of orders from a court of competent jurisdiction in the U.S.

cases.case_name: Nithya Anand Raghavan v. State (NCT of Delhi) and another
cases.principle: For the quintessence of the legal exposition on the issue.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a person is the guardian of a child, it is presumed that the custody of the child with that person is lawful.
obiter: A court order is only one of the factors to be taken into consideration.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in law and on facts by ordering the immediate restoration of the child's custody to the mother. The High Court failed to conduct an adequate examination of the facts and circumstances concerning the child's welfare, which is the paramount consideration. Instead, it was improperly impelled by the principle of comity of courts and related doctrines. The Court concluded that the father's custody was not illegal, a writ of habeas corpus was inappropriate, and dislodging the child from the father's care would be harmful to the child's interests.
legal_tests_applied: The sole and predominant criterion in custody matters is what would best serve the interest and welfare of the minor, which is of paramount significance.
In custody matters involving a parent, a writ of habeas corpus is not justified if the custody is not illegal or unlawful. Custody by a biological father is not, by itself, illegal or unlawful.
Courts exercise a parens patriae jurisdiction in custody matters, with an obligation to secure the unreserved welfare of the child.
The principles of comity of courts, "intimate contact," and "closest concern" are subordinate to the paramount consideration of the child's welfare.
There is no forum conveniens in wardship jurisdiction.
why_appellant_lost: The High Court did not at all apply itself to examine the facts and circumstances and the other materials on record bearing on the welfare and well-being of the child which unmistakeably is of paramount and decisive bearing.
The High Court seems to have been impelled by the principle of comity of courts and the doctrines of 'intimate contact' and 'closest concern' de hors thereto [the child's welfare].

No material has been brought on record, persuasive and convincing enough, to take a view that immediate restoration of the custody of the child to the respondent-mother in the native country is obligatorily called for in its interest and welfare.
why_respondent_won: The appellant being the biological father of Aadvik, his custody of the child can by no means in law be construed as illegal or unlawful drawing the invocation ofa superior Court's jurisdiction to issue a writ in the nature of habeas corpus.
The dislodgment of the child as directed by the impugned decision would be harmful to it.

The child, till he attains majority, ought to continue in the custody, charge and care of the appellant, subject to any order to the contrary, if passed by a court of competent jurisdiction in an appropriate proceeding deciding the issue of its custody in accordance with law.
policy_considerations: In such matters, the custody must be decided not by reference to the legal rights of the parties but on the sole and predominant criterion as to what would best serve the interest and welfare of the minor.
The peremptory mandate that underlines the adjudicative mission is the obligation to secure the unreserved welfare of the child as the paramount consideration.
The High Court would exercise its parens patriae jurisdiction, as the minor is within its jurisdiction.
